title: Locus
tagline: The set of points satisfying a given geometric condition, and its application to standard loci.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition. Instead of focusing on a single point, we describe a whole collection of points that share a property. This chapter develops the skill of translating geometric conditions into algebraic equations or descriptions of loci, and then uses those loci to solve problems involving intersections, distances, and positions. The four standard loci covered are: a point at a fixed distance from a given point (circle), a point at a fixed distance from a given line (two parallel lines), a point equidistant from two given points (perpendicular bisector), and a point equidistant from two given lines (angle bisectors).

facts.label: Locus of points at a fixed distance from a fixed point
facts.value: A circle with the point as centre and the distance as radius

facts.label: Locus of points equidistant from two fixed points
facts.value: The perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining the two points

facts.label: Locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines
facts.value: The pair of angle bisectors of the angles formed by the lines

facts.label: Locus of points moving such that its distances from two fixed points are always equal
facts.value: The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points

learningOutcomes: Define a locus and state the four standard loci studied in ICSE Class X.
Derive the equation or geometric description of a given locus from its defining condition.
Find the intersection of two loci and interpret the result geometrically.
Apply the locus concept to solve problems involving distance, equidistance, and position.
Distinguish between a locus and its graph: the locus is the set, the graph is the visual representation.
Verify a claimed locus point by substituting into the defining condition.

blocks.text: In geometry, a locus (plural: loci) is a set of points that share a common property. The condition that defines the locus could be a distance condition, an equidistance condition, or a relationship with a line or curve. For example, the locus of points that are always 5 cm from a fixed point P is a circle with centre P and radius 5 cm. The important thing to remember is that a locus describes an entire collection of points, not just one point. Every point on the locus satisfies the condition, and every point that satisfies the condition lies on the locus.

Locus questions appear in two main forms. In the first, you are given a condition and asked to describe the locus: "Describe the locus of points in the plane that are at a fixed distance from a given line." In the second, you are given a geometric construction and asked to identify the locus: "In the diagram, PA = PB. Describe the locus of point P." In both cases, the method is the same: state the condition in words, then recognise the standard locus it describes.

items.text: State the locus of points in a plane that are at a distance of 3 cm from a given point O.
items.note: The locus is a circle with centre O and radius 3 cm.

items.text: State the locus of points equidistant from two points A and B.
items.note: The locus is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB.

items.text: State the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines.
items.note: The locus is the pair of straight lines that bisect the angles between the given lines.

items.meaning: The set of all points satisfying a given condition.
The line that is perpendicular to a segment and passes through its midpoint.
The line that divides an angle into two equal angles.
The locus of points at a fixed distance (radius) from a centre point.

items: A locus is a set, not a single point.
Every point on the locus satisfies the defining condition.
Every point satisfying the condition lies on the locus.
The four standard loci are: circle, perpendicular bisector, angle bisectors, and parallel lines.

blocks.text: Every locus question in ICSE Class X Mathematics reduces to one of four standard cases. Being able to recognise which case applies is the key to solving the problem quickly and correctly.

items.text: Locus: distance from a fixed point is constant.
items.note: This is a circle. The fixed point is the centre, and the constant distance is the radius.

items.text: Locus: distance from a fixed line is constant.
items.note: This gives two parallel lines, one on each side of the given line, at the given distance.

items.text: Locus: equidistant from two fixed points.
items.note: This is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points.

items.text: Locus: equidistant from two intersecting lines.
items.note: This gives two angle bisectors, which are perpendicular to each other.

blocks.caption: The four standard loci and their geometric descriptions
rows: Distance from a fixed point is constant
Circle with the point as centre
Distance from a fixed line is constant
Two lines parallel to the given line
Line perpendicular to the segment through its midpoint
Two lines that bisect the angles between the given lines

blocks.text: The table captures all four standard loci in one place. When solving a locus problem, match the given condition to one of these four rows. If the condition does not match any row, re-read the question carefully — it may combine two conditions, in which case the locus is the intersection of two standard loci.

The most common type of locus problem asks for the intersection of two loci. For example: "Find the locus of points that are at a fixed distance from a given point AND equidistant from two given points." The answer is the point(s) where the two loci meet. In practice, this often means finding the intersection of a circle and a line, or the intersection of two perpendicular bisectors. The number of intersection points depends on the relative positions of the loci: they may intersect in two points, one point (tangent), or no real points.

items.text: Find the points that are 5 cm from point A and also equidistant from points A and B, given that AB = 8 cm.
items.note: The locus 5 cm from A is a circle centred at A with radius 5. The locus equidistant from A and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Since AB = 8 cm, the perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint of AB, which is 4 cm from A. The circle of radius 5 meets the bisector at two points, forming a right triangle with sides 3, 4, 5.

items.text: Find the locus of points inside a rectangle that are equidistant from two adjacent sides.
items.note: The locus is the set of points whose distances from the two sides are equal. This is the line at 45° that passes through the vertex where the sides meet, but only the part of the line that lies inside the rectangle.

items: To find the intersection of two loci, sketch or describe each locus and locate their common points.
The intersection of a circle and a line can be 0, 1, or 2 points.
The intersection of two perpendicular bisectors is a single point (the circumcentre of the triangle formed by the three points).
Always verify that intersection points satisfy both locus conditions.

learn.title: Constructing Loci with Ruler and Compass

blocks.text: Several of the standard loci can be constructed using only a ruler and compass. This section describes the practical construction alongside the theoretical description.

items.text: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a given line segment AB.
items.note: Step 1: With centre A and radius greater than half AB, draw a circle. Step 2: With centre B and the same radius, draw another circle intersecting the first at two points C and D. Step 3: Draw the line CD. This line is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

items.text: Construct the bisector of a given angle ABC.
items.note: Step 1: With centre B, draw a circle cutting the arms BA and BC at points E and F. Step 2: With centres E and F and the same radius, draw two circles intersecting at point G. Step 3: Draw the line BG. This line is the angle bisector.

items.text: Construct a circle given its centre and a point on the circle.
items.note: Step 1: Place the compass point on the centre. Step 2: Place the pencil on the given point. Step 3: Rotate the compass full circle, drawing the circle.

items: All constructions must be done with ruler and compass only (no protractor or set-square).
The pencil must not be lifted from the paper during a construction step.
Construction lines (arcs and rays) should be visible in the final diagram.
Always verify your construction by measurement.

learn.title: Checking a Point on a Locus

blocks.text: To verify that a point P lies on a given locus, substitute P into the defining condition and confirm that the condition is satisfied. For example, to verify that point (3, 4) lies on the circle with centre (0, 0) and radius 5, check that 3² + 4² = 5², which is true. To verify that a point does NOT lie on a locus, show that the condition fails.

items.text: Verify that the point (1, 2) lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (–1, 5) and (5, –1).
items.note: The midpoint of (–1, 5) and (5, –1) is (2, 2). The slope of the segment is (–1 – 5) / (5 – (–1)) = –6 / 6 = –1, so the perpendicular slope is 1. The line through (2, 2) with slope 1 has equation y – 2 = 1(x – 2), that is y = x. The point (1, 2) does not satisfy y = x (since 2 ≠ 1), so it is not on the perpendicular bisector.

items.text: Verify that the point (–2, –1) lies on the locus of points equidistant from (0, 0) and (3, 4).
items.note: Distance from (–2, –1) to (0, 0) = √((–2)² + (–1)²) = √5. Distance from (–2, –1) to (3, 4) = √((3 – (–2))² + (4 – (–1))²) = √(25 + 25) = √50. Since √5 ≠ √50, the point does not lie on the locus.

items: Substitute the point's coordinates into the locus equation or condition.
If the equation balances, the point is on the locus.
If the equation does not balance, the point is not on the locus.
Check both coordinates; a single sign error can change the result.

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from identifying standard loci through computing intersections to constructing loci and checking locus points. Work each one by recognising which of the four standard loci applies, then apply the appropriate method.

items: Identify the standard locus type before attempting any construction or calculation.
Distinguish between the locus itself and its intersection with another locus.
For coordinate-locus problems, write the equation of the locus before finding intersections.
Verify every claimed locus point by substitution.
In construction problems, state each step with its geometric justification.

keyPoints: A locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition; it is not a single point.
The four standard loci are: a circle, two parallel lines, a perpendicular bisector, and a pair of angle bisectors.
The locus of points at a fixed distance from a fixed point is a circle with that point as centre.
The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is the pair of angle bisectors of the angles they form.
The locus of points at a fixed distance from a given line is a pair of lines parallel to it.
The intersection of two loci is found by locating the common points of the two described sets.
A point is verified to lie on a locus by substituting it into the defining condition.
examFocus: When a question asks for the locus of points satisfying a stated condition, name the locus exactly and state the condition it satisfies.
For equidistance conditions, distinguish between two fixed points, which give a perpendicular bisector, and two intersecting lines, which give angle bisectors.
When a locus is a pair of lines, mention both of them; giving only one is incomplete.
For intersection problems, first describe each locus separately, then find their common points and check both conditions.
In construction problems, state each step and, where the question asks, give the geometric reason for the step.
When working with coordinates, verify a claimed locus point by substitution rather than by relying on a diagram alone.

vocabulary.meaning: The set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition.
The line perpendicular to a segment that passes through its midpoint; the locus of points equidistant from the segment's endpoints.
A line that divides an angle into two equal angles.
At equal distance from two or more given objects.
The set of points that belong to two given loci at the same time.
A point that stays in place under a given transformation.
A geometric drawing made with ruler and compass, with each step justified.

questions.prompt: The locus of points in a plane at a fixed distance from a given point is a:
questions.answer: circle
questions.explanation: By definition, a circle is the locus of points in a plane at a fixed (constant) distance from a fixed point, called the centre.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the locus with an ellipse, which requires two fixed points.

questions.prompt: The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points A and B is the:
questions.answer: perpendicular bisector of AB
questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector of a segment is the set of all points in the plane that are equidistant from the segment's endpoints.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it the median, which joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

questions.prompt: The locus of points in a plane at a constant distance of 4 cm from a given line L is ______.
questions.answer: two straight lines parallel to L
questions.explanation: A point moving so that its perpendicular distance from line L is always 4 cm traces out two lines parallel to L, one on each side at a distance of 4 cm.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one parallel line instead of two.

questions.prompt: The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is ______.
questions.answer: the pair of angle bisectors of the angles between the lines
questions.explanation: A point equidistant from two intersecting lines lies on one of the two angle bisectors that divide the angles into equal parts. The two bisectors are perpendicular to each other.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one angle bisector instead of the pair.

questions.prompt: State the locus of points in a plane at a constant distance of 5 cm from a fixed point P.
questions.answer: A circle with centre P and radius 5 cm.
questions.explanation: By definition, the locus of points in a plane that are a constant distance from a fixed point is a circle. Here the fixed point is P and the constant distance is 5 cm, so the locus is a circle with centre P and radius 5 cm.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only one point, or giving the centre correctly but forgetting to mention that the locus is a circle.

questions.prompt: Describe the locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines L1 and L2.
questions.answer: A straight line parallel to both L1 and L2 and midway between them.
questions.explanation: A point exactly halfway between two parallel lines is equidistant from them, and every such point lies on the unique line parallel to both and centered between them. Points on either side of this middle line are closer to one of the original lines than to the other.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the locus is a point or two lines instead of the single midway line.

questions.prompt: A point P moves so that its distances from two fixed points A and B are always equal. Describe the locus of P.
questions.answer: The perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB.
questions.explanation: The condition PA = PB means P is equidistant from A and B. The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, so the locus here is that perpendicular bisector.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing this with the midpoint only, when the locus is the entire perpendicular bisector line.

questions.prompt: Find the points that are 5 cm from point A and also equidistant from A and B, given that AB = 6 cm.
questions.answer: Two points, each lying on the perpendicular bisector of AB at a distance of 4 cm from the midpoint.
questions.explanation: The locus 5 cm from A is a circle centred at A with radius 5. The locus equidistant from A and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Since AB = 6 cm, the perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint M of AB, with AM = 3 cm. In the right triangle with hypotenuse 5 cm and one side 3 cm, the other side is 4 cm, so the two points lie on the perpendicular bisector at a distance of 4 cm from M. This gives two points, not one.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one intersection point or forgetting that the circle meets the perpendicular bisector in two points.

questions.prompt: A and B are two fixed points 10 cm apart. Find the locus of points P such that PA = PB and PA = 8 cm.
questions.answer: Two points, each on the perpendicular bisector of AB at a distance of √(8² − 5²) = √39 cm from the midpoint.
questions.explanation: PA = PB means P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, which passes through the midpoint M of AB with AM = 5 cm. PA = 8 cm then gives, in the right triangle PMA, PM = √(PA² − AM²) = √(8² − 5²) = √(64 − 25) = √39 cm. There are two such points, one on each side of AB along the perpendicular bisector.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to compute PM from the right triangle or giving only the midpoint as the locus.

questions.prompt: Which points are invariant under reflection in a given line?
questions.answer: The points lying on the line itself.
questions.explanation: A reflection in a line maps a point to its mirror image on the opposite side of the line. If a point already lies on the line, its mirror image coincides with it, so it is invariant. No point off the line is invariant.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the origin is invariant in every case, when invariance depends on the mirror line.

questions.prompt: A point P moves so that its distance from A(2, 1) is always equal to its distance from B(8, 5). Find the equation of the locus of P and describe it geometrically.
questions.answer: The locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB; its equation is 3x + 2y = 21.
questions.explanation: Let P(x, y). PA = PB gives (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² = (x − 8)² + (y − 5)². Expanding: x² − 4x + 4 + y² − 2y + 1 = x² − 16x + 64 + y² − 10y + 25. Cancelling x² and y² gives −4x − 2y + 5 = −16x − 10y + 89. Rearranging: 12x + 8y = 84, and dividing by 4 gives 3x + 2y = 21. This is the equation of a straight line, and it is the perpendicular bisector of AB because it consists of all points equidistant from A and B. The midpoint of AB, (5, 3), satisfies 3(5) + 2(3) = 15 + 6 = 21, confirming it lies on the locus.
questions.commonMistake: Expanding (x − a)² incorrectly as x² − a², or failing to keep the sign of the linear terms correct.

questions.prompt: Find the locus of points equidistant from the lines y = 2 and y = 8.
questions.answer: The line y = 5.
questions.explanation: The distance from a point (x, y) to the line y = 2 is |y − 2|, and to the line y = 8 is |y − 8|. Setting these equal gives |y − 2| = |y − 8|. Squaring or reasoning geometrically, the points equally distant from two parallel horizontal lines lie on the horizontal line midway between them, which is y = (2 + 8)/2 = 5. Thus the locus is the line y = 5.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the locus as a single point or as two lines instead of the single midway line.

questions.prompt: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment AB of length 7 cm. State the steps and the geometric reason for the construction.
questions.answer: Steps: (1) With centre A, draw a circle of radius greater than 3.5 cm; (2) With centre B and the same radius, draw a circle intersecting the first at C and D; (3) Draw the line CD. Reason: C and D are each equidistant from A and B, so CD is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
questions.explanation: The two circles have equal radii, so C and D are both at the same distance from A and from B. A point equidistant from A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so both C and D lie on that perpendicular bisector. The line through them is therefore the perpendicular bisector. Because the radius is greater than half AB, the circles intersect in two points and the line CD can be drawn.
questions.commonMistake: Using a radius shorter than half AB, which makes the circles fail to intersect.

questions.prompt: The locus of the centre of a swinging door that rotates about a fixed hinge is:
questions.answer: a circle
questions.explanation: The hinge is a fixed point and the centre of the door stays at a fixed distance from it as the door swings, so the locus of that centre is a circle with the hinge as its centre.
questions.commonMistake: Imagining the door opening in a straight line rather than rotating about the hinge.

questions.prompt: Describe the locus of the centre of a wheel of a bicycle moving in a straight line along a horizontal road.
questions.answer: A straight line parallel to the road, at a height equal to the radius of the wheel above the road.
questions.explanation: The centre of the wheel stays at a fixed perpendicular distance from the road equal to the wheel's radius, and it moves horizontally as the bicycle moves. The set of all such positions is a straight line parallel to the road. If the bicycle changes direction, the locus becomes a curve rather than a straight line.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the locus is the road itself, when the centre is above the road by the radius.

questions.prompt: The locus of the midpoint of a line segment of constant length that slides with its ends on two perpendicular lines is ______.
questions.answer: a circle
questions.explanation: If the ends are on two perpendicular axes and the segment has constant length 2a, the midpoint stays at a fixed distance a from the intersection of the axes, so its locus is a circle with that intersection as centre and radius a. This is a standard locus that appears in several textbook forms.
questions.commonMistake: Giving a straight line because the ends move along straight lines.

questions.prompt: A point P moves so that the sum of its distances from two fixed points A and B is constant. Is its locus one of the four standard loci of ICSE Class X? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: No. The locus is an ellipse, not one of the four standard loci.
questions.explanation: The four standard loci are: a circle, two parallel lines, a perpendicular bisector, and a pair of angle bisectors. The condition PA + PB = constant defines an ellipse with foci A and B, not a circle or a line. An ellipse is not part of the ICSE Class X locus list, so while the condition is meaningful, it does not reduce to one of the standard loci of this chapter.
questions.commonMistake: Calling the locus a circle, which would require PA to be constant rather than PA + PB.

questions.prompt: A point P moves so that its distance from A(0, 0) is always twice its distance from B(3, 0). Find the equation of the locus of P.
questions.answer: The locus is the circle x² + y² − 8x + 12 = 0.
questions.explanation: Let P(x, y). PA = 2 PB gives PA² = 4 PB², so x² + y² = 4[(x − 3)² + y²] = 4(x² − 6x + 9 + y²) = 4x² − 24x + 36 + 4y². Rearranging: 0 = 3x² − 24x + 36 + 3y², and dividing by 3 gives x² − 8x + 12 + y² = 0, or x² + y² − 8x + 12 = 0. Completing the square for x gives (x − 4)² + y² = 4, which is a circle with centre (4, 0) and radius 2.
questions.commonMistake: Writing PA = 2 PB as PA = PB + PB and treating it as a linear condition instead of squaring.

questions.prompt: A point P moves so that its distance from a fixed point O is always 6 cm. What is the locus of P, and what is its radius and centre?
questions.answer: The locus is a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm.
questions.explanation: The set of all points at a constant distance from a fixed point is a circle. Here the fixed point is O and the constant distance is 6 cm, so the locus is a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm.
questions.commonMistake: Naming the locus correctly but forgetting to state both the centre and the radius as asked.

questions.prompt: A point P moves so that its distance from a fixed line l is always 3 cm. How many lines make up the locus?
questions.answer: Two lines, one on each side of l, each parallel to l at a distance of 3 cm.
questions.explanation: A point whose perpendicular distance from a fixed line l is always 3 cm can lie either 3 cm above l or 3 cm below l, giving two lines parallel to l. Both satisfy the condition, so the locus has two lines rather than one.
questions.commonMistake: Drawing only one parallel line and forgetting the one on the opposite side of l.

questions.prompt: The locus of points equidistant from the arms of an angle is:
options: the perpendicular bisector of one arm
a circle centred at the vertex
a line parallel to one arm
questions.answer: the angle bisector
questions.explanation: A point inside the angle that is equidistant from the two arms lies on the line that bisects the angle. This is one of the four standard loci: the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is the pair of angle bisectors.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the angle bisector with the perpendicular bisector of one arm.

questions.prompt: A and B are two fixed points. Find the locus of points P such that angle APB is a right angle.
questions.answer: The locus is the circle with AB as diameter, excluding A and B.
questions.explanation: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so if APB = 90° then P must lie on the circle that has AB as diameter. The converse also holds: any point P on that circle, other than A and B, gives a right angle APB. Therefore the locus is the circle on AB as diameter, with A and B themselves excluded because the angle is not defined there.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting the fact that A and B themselves are excluded, or describing the locus as only the midpoint.

questions.prompt: The number of common points of a circle and a line can be:
questions.explanation: A line can miss a circle entirely, giving 0 common points; it can touch the circle, giving 1 common point (tangent); or it can cut through the circle, giving 2 common points (a secant). All three cases occur in locus intersection problems.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming a line and a circle always meet in two points.
